factsAccepted: Earned/realized ROE declined from 9.5% (FY2023) to 8.9% (FY2024) to 8.2% (FY2025), now ~160 bps below the 9.8% allowed ROE authorized in the last rate case. With equity at ~50% of the $9,000M rate base (~$4,500M), a 160 bps under-earning implies an annual earnings shortfall of roughly 1.6% x $4,500M ≈ $72M relative to the authorized return. EBITDA is stable; the erosion is in realized return on deployed capital, not in revenue or operating profit volatility.

Approved/realized revenue grew 2.4% YoY (FY2024 $2,930M to FY2025 $3,000M), within the PUC-allowed 2-3% band, while the unit cost of the capital program inflated ~9% YoY. This is a ~660 bps gap between the rate at which approved revenue can grow and the rate at which the cost of the capital being added is rising — the regulated price mechanism is growing far slower than the cost it is meant to recover on incremental capital.

Annual capex is $1,100M against depreciation of ~$650M, a capex/depreciation ratio of 1.69x, so the rate base is expanding far faster than recovery through current rates. The capital plan is driven by grid hardening, reliability, and decarbonization mandates and grows the rate base from $9,000M to ~$10,200M (+13%) over the plan horizon. Meanwhile O&M is run lean and is roughly flat, so the under-earning is a capital-recovery problem, not an operating-expense problem.

Rates are reset only every ~3 years and are based on a historical test year; current rates reflect a test year that is ~24 months old by the time they take effect. As a result, by the time rates are in effect they already understate the cost of capital deployed since the test year, producing chronic regulatory lag and under-recovery between cases. The next rate-case filing window opens in ~120-180 days; the choice of test-year convention (historical vs forward) and recovery mechanisms (trackers/riders) in that filing largely determines the realized return for the next ~3-year cycle.

Retail demand and customer count are stable (~1.6M customers); load growth is modest and broadly in line with the 2-3% allowed revenue band. There is no evidence of a demand collapse or volume-driven revenue loss — sales volumes are steady. This rules out a demand/forecasting explanation for the return erosion and isolates the driver to the rate-versus-capital-cost mechanism.
factsNeedingClarification: The PUC's internal disposition / likelihood of approving a forward test year or specific tracker mechanisms in the next case (not disclosable pre-filing)
Detailed cost-of-service study allocations by customer class beyond the last filed case (proprietary / not yet filed)
Confidential settlement positions of intervenors and consumer advocates for the upcoming case
Forward interest-rate path and its effect on the next authorized cost of capital (market-dependent, not disclosed)
Project-by-project deferral flexibility within the mandated capital plan (internal engineering assessments not public)
